title: Finding the refractive index of an unknown material
file: 1C Practical 1C–1 Finding the refractive index of an unknown material.docx
aim: The aim of this practical activity is to calculate the refractive index of an unknown material by comparing the incident and reflected rays. Pre-lab questions 1.  What is the difference between reflection and refraction?
materials: Hodson light box
Battery pack or power supply
Lenses
Single slit plate
Paper protractors (2 semi-circle images or one full circular image)
Pencil
Graph paper
method: Set up the Hodson light box with a single slit adjacent to the light source.
Place a paper protractor with the rounded edge facing the light in front of the light box.
Place a second protractor so it makes a full circle. Alternatively, print the image in the appendix to use as a protractor.
Initially aim the light along the normal (at 90 degrees) so that with no change the light will continue along the line of the normal.
Place the transparent object that you are measuring at the diameter of the protractor circle.
Modify the angle of incidence to all angles between 10 and 80 degrees. Keep in mind 10 degrees means 10 away from 90 and so on. You must calculate from the normal.
Record the angle of refraction for each from your paper protractor.
Graph the sin  (i)  against the sin  (r)  for your calculations. Find the gradient of this graph. This will give you the refractive index of the unknown material.
Research what the material might be made of based on the refractive index you calculate.

title: Convection in water
aim: To make the convective flow in water visible and to investigate the conditions under which convection occurs in a liquid.
materials: Bunsen burner for Part 1
200 mL beaker
A straw or thin rigid tube
Tweezers
Crystals of potassium permanganate (KMnO₄)
Retort stand and heatproof mat
Heat lamp for Part 2 (or a desk lamp with incandescent bulb of at least 100 W)
Ice cubes for Part 3
Plastic bag and string or twist-ties for Part 3
safety: Care should be taken when using Bunsen burners and heat lamps. Ensure that water is not spilled on the heat lamp. Be mindful that the beakers and water will be hot, so should be handled carefully and placed securely on the heatproof mat and retort stand. Allow it to cool before disposing of the permanganate solution.
method: Place the beaker of water on the retort stand.
Put the straw in the water (at an oblique angle).
Allow to stand undisturbed for 5 minutes.
Use tweezers to drop only 2 or 3 potassium permanganate crystals down the straw so they settle at the bottom of the beaker, to the side.
Carefully withdraw the straw, avoiding disturbing the water.
Place the Bunsen burner to the beaker under the crystals, and light it.
Observe and sketch the direction of currents in the water, inferred from movement of the purple colour.
Place a beaker of fresh water on the bench.
Place the heat lamp (turned off) so that it will shine on the top of the water surface.
Use same procedure as in Part 1 Steps 2–5 with crystals and straw.
Turn on the lamp.
Observe and sketch the direction of inferred currents in the water as before.
Place a beaker of fresh lukewarm water on the bench, with a retort stand over it.
Follow Steps 2–5 of Part 1.

Place some ice cubes in a plastic bag, squeeze out the air, and tie it closed with the string or twist-tie. Gently immerse the plastic bag in the water above the potassium permanganate crystals, so it hangs just below the water surface, and tie it to the retort stand.
Observe and sketch the direction of inferred currents in the water as before.
prelab: What explains the change of density with temperature?
Should liquid of lower density move up through liquid of higher density when the liquid is heated from below?
Should liquid be heated from above or below if you want to minimise the amount of energy used to heat it?
Explain whether a heating method that warms all parts of a liquid by the same amount at the same time, would result in convection currents.
Examining the patterns of convection and the efficiency of heating from below in contrast to from above

Compare the direction of the currents in Parts 1–3 of the experiment in the spaces below by drawing a diagram, including arrows for any currents observed and their direction. Below the diagram, summarise in words whether the water was heated or cooled at the top or the bottom, and describe any currents observed. (2 marks for each part)

title: Calculating half-life from a simulation
file: 3C Practical 3C–1 Calculating half-life from a simulation.docx
aim: To model the number of undecayed and decayed atoms in a radioactive isotope sample using a probability experiment, showing how the half-life of a radioisotope is calculated, and the effect of the size of the starting numbers. <Teacher note: Teachers should instruct students on the policy for eating/not eating the M&Ms used in this practical, e.g. ‘you can eat decayed M&Ms as you go’ (depending on whether any have to be reused), or ‘no eating of the M&Ms during the practical, at the end you can divide them up to eat in the break’.>
materials: 100 chocolate M&Ms (do not use peanut M&Ms), there are about 200 in a 180 g packet, so one packet should be enough for two groups. The trial 1 M&Ms could be re-used in trial 2, then only 80 will be needed for each group. (Other brands of lolly could be used, as long as they have an equal chance of landing on either side, i.e. they are symmetrical, and a mark that distinguishes the sides).
A cup
Clean sheets of paper or trays
Coloured pencils or textas for different plotlines on graphs
method: For trial 1, place 20 M&Ms into the cup.
Shake the cup and pour the M&M’s onto the paper or tray.

The M&Ms with the printed ‘M’ side up are regarded as ‘decayed’. Remove them from the trial and returning them to the packet. Record the number of ‘undecayed’ M&Ms remaining and in table in the Results section against ‘shake and pour’ event number 1. Record the next ‘shake and pour’ event as number 2, and so on.

Return the undecayed M&Ms to the cup and repeat Steps 2 and 3, recording the number of undecayed M&Ms in the table in the Results section against the shake and pour event number, until there are none left, or until 12 events have been carried out.
Repeat Steps 1–4 as the second trial, this time with 80 M&Ms.

Plot a graph of the results from the table in the Results section on the grid provided, using different colours for the plotlines of the two trials. Include a key. Note that the axis for trial 1 is on the left, the axis for trial 2 is on the right and they are not to the same scale. This is so the shape of the curves can be compared at the same size.
Use the graph to determine the half-life of M&Ms in terms of the number of pours.
prelab: 1 × 10⁶ atoms of a radioactive isotope start decaying and after 24 seconds there are 5 × 10⁵ undecayed atoms left. From this point, how long will it take on average for half of these to decay? Give your reasoning.
Is the decay of an atom in a sample of an isotope dependant on the decay of the neighbouring atoms?
A sample of a radioactive isotope decays for one half-life.
a.  After that time has elapsed, what is the chance that a single atom in the sample is observed to be decayed?
b.  Give an example of a simple probability trial (experiment) with two outcomes, a 50% chance of either happening and that could be used to model undecayed/decayed atoms in a sample.
Calculating half-life

title: Protection against radiation
aim: To investigate the shielding required for protection from external α-, β- and γ-radiation. <Teacher note: This practical requires the use of ionising radiation sources. Safety precautions are imperative. It may be done as a teacher demonstration rather than a student practical. See the safety notes below the material list. It is advisable to test the set-up with the sheets before the practical, to test the ideal distances of source, sheet and detector, so that the expected number of counts will be recorded in a minute.>
materials: Alpha, beta and gamma sources produced for school laboratory use, sealed and complete with safe handling instructions
Stand and clamp to hold source
Radiation detector with stand and clamp
Counter and powerpack for the detector
Sheets of cardboard, aluminium, lead and, at the teacher’s discretion, sheets of other materials such as cloth, polythene, rubber and a lead block
Stand to hold the sheets between source and detector. Some sheets may need to be held at the top rather than the bottom.
Tongs
Gloves
Stopwatch
Ruler
safety: -   Care should be taken when using radioactive sources. Since radiation is invisible, it is important to be aware of the dangers involved. -   Always handle radioactive sources with a pair of tongs and wear gloves. -   Avoid having the sources close to your body. -   Never damage the container in which the radioisotope is held. -   Make sure all radioactive sources are in a lead lined container when not in use.
method: Set up the apparatus as shown in the diagram below.

With all the radiation sources in their lead box, obtain a background radiation count by leaving the counter on for 3 minutes. Average this to calculate the number of counts per minute for the background value.

Place the alpha source (open side toward detector tube) about 5–10 mm away from the end of the detector tube and record the number of counts in 1 minute, as timed by the stopwatch. Subtract the background value from the recorded value to get the actual count from the source.

Now place a sheet of cardboard between the source and the tube. Record the counts in 1 minute and subtract the background count to get the actual count. Repeat this process with the other sheets chosen for the practical. Write names in the blank column headers in the table in the Results section.
Replace the alpha source with a beta source (radiation symbol toward detector) and repeat Steps 2 and 3.
Now replace the beta source with a gamma source (radiation symbol toward detector) and repeat Steps 2 and 3.
Also, using the lead block if required, determine how many millimetres of lead are required to effectively stop the gamma rays completely (i.e. reduce the count to the background level).
prelab: What type of particle or wave each comprises alpha, beta and gamma radiation?
What are the principal safety precautions around the use and handling of alpha, beta and gamma radiation sources?
What two physical properties of material used for shielding are most important in affecting the penetrating power of radiation from nuclear decay?
Protection against radiation
Summarise the minimum levels of shielding protection required (in terms of material) against the three types of ionising radiation in this practical. (3 marks)

Thinking about the role of shielding, what are the particular dangers of internal radiation? What does this mean for ingestion or inhalation of sources of α-, β- and γ-radiation, such as polonium-210 (an α-emitter) and lead-210 (a β-emitter) in cigarette smoke? (4 marks)

title: Nuclear fission simulation
aim: To use an online simulation of nuclear fission to understand the process and what factors affect its rate, and how it can be controlled in nuclear reactors. <Teacher note: This practical requires each student or group to have live access to an external website. It is recommended that teachers explore the simulator and familiarise themselves with it before the practical, since not all its features may work as expected. To avoid delays, it is also suggested that students check before the practical that they can access the site using the link below.>
materials: Pause ( || )and Play ( ) buttons
the red ‘fire’ button on the neutron gun (simulation must be playing)
the Reset Nucleus button which appears after firing.
to set the proportion of uranium-235 to uranium-238 nuclei (note some combinations aren’t possible)
to add a containment vessel
to read of the number of uranium-235 atoms fissioned
Note that if the fired neutron misses all the fissile nuclei, you can drag the mouth of the neutron gun to aim it.
the Control Rod Adjuster, the Fire Neutrons button and the Reset Nuclei button
the thermometer graphic display for temperature and the Energy Graphs pane.
method: Describe what happens when the uranium-235 nucleus is hit with a neutron. Use the Pause button when needed. Use Reset Nucleus to watch the process repeatedly.
What is emitted that is not included in the ‘Legend’ (key)?

U-235 100 Nuclei: Click the Reset All button and then set the initial number of uranium-235 nuclei to 100 and uranium-238 to 0. What happens when you fire the neutron gun (that differs from your answer to Part 1 Step 1)?
U-235 100 Nuclei: Explain what makes this a chain reaction.

Fewer U-235 nuclei: Continuing with the Containment Vessel box unticked and uranium-238 set to zero, explore using lower numbers of uranium-235. Try to find if there is a lowest number of uranium-235 nuclei that will produce a chain reaction that fissions all nuclei fission from firing one neutron.

U-238 100 Nuclei: Click Reset All and then set the initial number of uranium-238 nuclei to 100 and uranium-235 to 0. Explain what happens when you fire the gun. Try different numbers of uranium-238 nuclei, keeping uranium-235 to zero, and try to start a chain reaction with the uranium-238.

U-235 50 Nuclei and U-238 50 Nuclei: Click Reset All and set uranium-235 to 50 nuclei and uranium-238 to 50 nuclei. Aim the gun at a nearby cluster of uranium-235 and fire. Note the percentage of uranium-235 nuclei fissioned at the end. Repeat the simulation for five trials and say whether 100% of the uranium-235 nuclei fissioned in any of these.

Varying U-235 and U-238 nuclei numbers: Repeat Step 5 above, varying the numbers of uranium-235 and uranium-238 nuclei to find the highest number of uranium-238 and lowest number of uranium-235 where 100% of the uranium-235 are likely to fission. Describe and explain your findings.

Control rods fully inserted: Carry out three trials of firing the neutrons with the control rods fully inserted, noting where fission starts and proceeds and what was displayed in the energy bar graphs.

Control rods withdrawn halfway: Carry out three trials of firing the neutrons with the control rods withdrawn halfway, noting where fission starts and proceeds and what was displayed in the energy bar graphs.

Control rods fully withdrawn: Carry out three trials of firing the neutrons with the control rods fully withdrawn, noting where fission starts and proceeds and what was displayed in the energy bar graphs.

Control rods fully withdrawn then reinserted: Carry out three trials of firing the neutrons with the control rods fully withdrawn and watch the temperature display. When the temperature exceeds the halfway mark on the thermometer, quickly insert the control rods fully and note what happens.
prelab: What is a chain reaction?
What do control rods do in a nuclear reactor to control the reaction, and how can a nuclear fission chain reaction be slowed and even stopped completely?

In the naturally occurring ores of an element, there is frequently more than one isotope present. What is the name of the process that increases the proportion of the desirable isotope in the element, and why is this done in the case of uranium?
Nuclear fission simulation
In the simulations, after a nucleus fission, there are loose neutrons flying about.
a.  What happens when a loose neutron hits a uranium-235, uranium-238 and uranium-239 nucleus? (3 marks)

title: Voltage across a thermistor
aim: To show the change in output voltages of a circuit with a variable resistor in series with a thermistor. In a simple electrical circuit comprising of a power supply, a thermistor and a variable resistor, measure the voltage across variable resistor, and across the thermistor for varying temperatures of a water bath containing the thermistor.
materials: Electrical power supply
Wires with plugs or clips (or a prepared circuit board)
Thermistor
Water bath
Variable resistor
Voltmeter(s) (or multimeters)
A source of water of differing temperatures
Thermometer (analogue or digital)
safety: Care should be taken when using electricity. Even low-voltage sources will produce a spark or mild shock. When using a multimeter, ensure the correct mode (voltmeter or ammeter) is selected before turning on and before connecting in the circuit, otherwise ammeter mode incorrectly positioned in the circuit could short-circuit the load.
method: Connect the elements as shown in the circuit diagram below.
Set the variable resistor []at some low value (but not zero).
Place the thermistor in a bath of iced water.
Select a supply voltage that is not more than the nominal operating voltage of the thermistor.
Do not turn on the power supply until the circuit has been checked by the teacher.
Measure (in the position marked ‘V’ on the circuit diagram) the voltage using the voltmeter (or the multimeter switched to voltmeter mode) across the thermistor.
Move the voltmeter (or use a second voltmeter if available) to measure the voltage across the variable resistor.
Measure the temperature of the water.
Repeat Steps 6, 7 and 8 with water at room temperature in the bath.
Repeat Steps 6, 7 and 8 with water at near boiling temperature.
Refill the bath with water at room temperature.
Increase slightly the resistance of the variable resistor.
Measure (in the position marked ‘V’ on the circuit diagram) the voltage using the voltmeter (or the multimeter switched to voltmeter mode) across the thermistor.
Move the voltmeter (or use a second voltmeter if available) to measure the voltage across the variable resistor.
Measure the temperature of the water.
Increase the resistance of the variable resistor to about half of the maximum.
Repeat Steps 13, 14 and 15.
Increase the resistance of the variable resistor to near maximum.
Repeat Steps 13, 14 and 15.
prelab: For constant supply voltage in a circuit that includes a series resistor, what effect does increasing the temperature of the NTC thermistor have on the output voltage, V_(out), across the thermistor?
If the circuit described in Question 1 is at constant temperature, what effect does increasing the resistance on the variable resistor have on the voltage, V_(out), of the thermistor?
Voltage across a thermistor
What is the relationship between temperature and output voltage across the thermistor? Why? (2 marks)
What is the relationship between the voltages across the variable resistor and across the thermistor at constant temperature? Why? (2 marks)

The resistance of the NTC thermistor decreases for increasing temperature, so the resistance of the thermistor will be a decreasing fraction of the total resistance of the circuit. Therefore, the voltage across the thermistor will decrease. (2 marks).

title: Water rockets
aim: Find the volume of water in a water rocket that will give the greatest flight duration or height.
materials: Stopwatch, clinometer or both
Water bottle rocket (see diagram above) including a plastic soda bottle with fins attached
Launch tube or other type of launcher to which the bottle and air pump can be attached

Water

safety: -   All students must wear safety glasses at all times. -   The launch tube or other launch device must be placed securely in the ground so that it points vertically upwards without leaning or falling over. -   Students must not angle the rockets at any angle other than 90° to the ground at all times, especially when pressurised. -   Students should not exceed a maximum pressure of 50 psi (3.5 bar) on the pump’s air pressure gauge. If a rocket does not launch by the time the maximum is reached, students should consult the teacher to depressurise the rocket safely. -   All launches must be conducted in a space that is approximately a 30 m radius away from other people, trees and buildings. It is assumed that the same rocket and launcher will be used by all students. If more than one bottle rocket and launcher is available, they should be no closer than 30 m apart.
method: Measure the desired amount of water and place it into the water bottle.
Attach the bottle rocket, complete with fins, to the launch tube.
Attach the bike pump to the launch tube.
Secure the launch tube on the ground ensuring it is perpendicular to the horizontal, and that it cannot lean or fall over.
Pump at an even rate until the water bottle rocket launches. At least one person should observe the air pressure gauge and call a halt if the maximum is reached.
Measure the duration of flight using a stopwatch or measure the height of the rocket with a clinometer.
Repeat Steps 4–9 with varying amounts of water, as worked out at Step 3.
Results should be recorded in an appropriate table. The average flight duration or height reached should be calculated for each volume or mass of water used.

title: Newton’s second law
aim: To determine the effect of mass on acceleration.
materials: Low-friction cart

method: Measure the mass of the cart on the scales and record it in row 1 of the table in the Results section.

Record 3 trials.

title: Spring constants and elastic potential energy

aim: To find the spring constant and stored elastic potential energy for a 5 cm extension of three different springs.

method: Set up the first spring so that it is hanging vertically from an arm clamped to a retort stand and clamp as shown in the diagram below.
